title: A Policy-Heavy Issue with a Dash of Evolution
content: We have a letter by Schaldach and Wilde (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biaf005) and a response by O’Connell and colleagues (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biaf048), both in general agreement on the importance of field-centered undergraduate experiences but commenting on the original article by team O’Connell (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biab112) on how to constructively evaluate these pedagogies. Yang’s book review (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biaf006) of Lala and colleagues’ Evolution Evolving: The Developmental Origins of Adaptation and Biodiversity provides a cogent argument supportive of the authors’ contention that development should be included within the panoply of evolutionary process. An evolutionary perspective is also used by Glaberman and colleagues in their Viewpoint, “The evolutionary dilemma of broad-spectrum insecticides” (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biaf074), which makes the very reasonable argument that insecticides are likely to affect many target-related beneficial insects. The evolutionary answer is to design pesticides with more specific neurochemical targets.
